33: 
34: ## Overview
35: This project sets up, compiles, simulates, and serves an ESP32-based Network Attached Storage (NAS) and Static Web Server entirely on your local workstation using the **Wokwi for VS Code** extension and **PlatformIO IDE**.
36: 
37: By running simulation locally, the ESP32 code executes via your local compiler toolchain without cloud rate limits, and network requests can be bridged directly to your host PC loopback adapter (`localhost:9080`) as well as external network interfaces (wired Ethernet and wireless Mobile Hotspot).
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## Project Directory Structure
42: 
43: ```text
44: Project.MM/LocalConfig/
45: │
46: ├── .gitignore             # Ignores .pio/ build artifacts and local IDE files
47: ├── platformio.ini         # Toolchain & dependency configuration
48: ├── wokwi.toml             # Wokwi simulation descriptor
49: ├── diagram.json           # Circuit schematics and SPI pin mappings
50: ├── wokwigw.exe            # Local network gateway binary
51: ├── setup_firewall.bat     # One-click UAC auto-elevated Windows Firewall rule installer
52: ├── README.md              # Project documentation and execution instructions
53: ├── include/
54: │   └── html_templates.h   # Modular glassmorphic HTML/CSS templates & PROGMEM strings
55: └── src/
56:     └── main.cpp           # ESP32 C++ firmware code
57: ```
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## Prerequisites & Extension Setup
62: 
63: 1. **Install Visual Studio Code**: Ensure VS Code is installed.
64: 2. **Install Extensions**:
65:    - Open VS Code Extensions view (`Ctrl + Shift + X`).
66:    - Search for and install **Wokwi Simulator** (`wokwi.wokwi-vscode`).
67:    - Search for and install **PlatformIO IDE** (`platformio.platformio-ide`).
68: 3. *(Optional for first-time Wokwi setup)*: Press `F1`, type `Wokwi: Request License`, and claim your free trial/license token if prompted by the extension.
69: 
70: ---
71: 
72: ## Configuration Files Breakdown
73: 
74: ### 1. `platformio.ini`
75: Instructs PlatformIO to compile firmware targeting the standard ESP32 DevKit using the Arduino framework:
76: ```ini
77: [env:esp32dev]
78: platform = espressif32
79: board = esp32dev
80: framework = arduino
81: monitor_speed = 115200
82: 
83: ; Built-in libraries used directly: WiFi, WebServer, SPI, SD, FS
84: lib_deps =
85: ```
86: 
87: ### 2. `wokwi.toml`
88: Tells Wokwi where PlatformIO places the compiled binary and ELF debug symbols, and routes simulation network traffic through the local `wokwigw` gateway:
89: ```toml
90: [wokwi]
91: version = 1
92: firmware = ".pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin"
93: elf = ".pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.elf"
94: 
95: [net]
96: gateway = "ws://localhost:9011"
97: ```
98: *(The `[net]` block is required for `wokwigw` so that virtual Wi-Fi packets are forwarded through the local gateway at `localhost:9011`).*
99: 
100: 
101: ### 3. `diagram.json`
102: Specifies virtual hardware and hardware SPI wiring (using Wokwi `D`-prefixed silkscreen pin names):
103: - **`wokwi-esp32-devkit-v1`**: Core MCU board.
104: - **`wokwi-microsd-card`**: SPI MicroSD card module.
105: - **Pin Connections**:
106:   - `esp:3V3` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:VCC`
107:   - `esp:GND.1` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:GND`
108:   - `esp:D5` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:CS` (Chip Select)
109:   - `esp:D23` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:DI` (MOSI)
110:   - `esp:D19` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:DO` (MISO)
111:   - `esp:D18` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:SCK` (Serial Clock)
112: 
113: ### 4. `include/html_templates.h`
114: Modular UI templates:
115: - Contains glassmorphic dark UI CSS styles, responsive layouts, storage bar templates, and the static website template (`SEED_INDEX_HTML`).
116: - Stored directly in Flash ROM using `PROGMEM` and C++ raw string literals `R"rawliteral(...)rawliteral"`, keeping internal SRAM free.
117: 
118: ### 5. `src/main.cpp`
119: Firmware architecture:
120: - **Phase 1 Storage**: Explicitly initializes `SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, 5)` and mounts FAT32 SD filesystem via `SD.begin(5, SPI)`. Automatically seeds `/www/index.html` and `/lab_report.txt` and enumerates files.
121: - **Phase 2 Networking**: Connects to `Wokwi-GUEST` Wi-Fi, hosts web endpoints on port 80 (`/`, `/site`, `/get`, `/upload`, `/delete`), and executes automated internal self-diagnostics on FreeRTOS Core 1.
122: 
123: ### 6. `setup_firewall.bat`
124: Automated administrative script:
125: - Automatically requests UAC elevation if not launched as Administrator.
126: - Executes `New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Wokwi Gateway NAS" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 9080 -Protocol TCP -Profile Any -Action Allow` to permit inbound traffic on port 9080 across all network profiles (Domain, Private, Public).
127: - Guarantees wired Ethernet LAN peers and wireless Mobile Hotspot devices can access the server without connection timeouts.
128: 
129: > [!TIP]
130: > - For a complete project show walkthrough, oral defense script, and architectural Q&A, refer to the **[Presentation Guide](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/PRESENTATION_GUIDE.md)**.
131: > - For automated one-click dependency installation, automated build scripts, and offline tools, check out [`Project.MM/setup/`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/setup) and [`Project.MM/setup/SETUP_GUIDE.md`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/setup/SETUP_GUIDE.md).
132: 
133: ---
134: 
135: ## Step-by-Step Simulation Execution
136: 
137: ### Step 1: Open the Project in VS Code
138: Open the directory `Project.MM/LocalConfig` directly in VS Code (`File` > `Open Folder...`). This ensures PlatformIO immediately detects `platformio.ini` and Wokwi automatically loads [`wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml).
139: 
140: > [!NOTE]
141: > **If VS Code was opened at the repo root (`Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab`)** instead of `Project.MM/LocalConfig`, make sure Wokwi uses [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml) by pressing `F1` $\rightarrow$ **`Wokwi: Select Config File`** (or reopen `Project.MM/LocalConfig` directly as the workspace folder). Otherwise, Wokwi may fail to load the `[net]` gateway setting or the compiled firmware binary.
142: 
143: ### Step 2: Compile the Firmware
144: - Click the **PlatformIO Build checkmark (✓)** on the bottom blue status bar, or press `Ctrl + Alt + B`.
145: - PlatformIO will download toolchains and libraries on first run, compiling to `.pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin`.
146: 
147: ### Step 3: Configure Windows Firewall (One-Click)
148: To ensure client devices (such as smartphones and lab desktop PCs) can reach port 9080:
149: - Double-click [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) (or run from terminal).
150: - Accept the Windows UAC elevation prompt. The script configures inbound TCP port 9080 across all network profiles automatically.
151: 
152: ### Step 4: Launch Network Gateway (wokwigw)
153: In a terminal window (PowerShell) inside `Project.MM/LocalConfig`:
154: ```powershell
155: .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
156: ```
157: *(Leave this running in the background. It forwards host port 9080 into the simulated ESP32 port 80).*
158: 
159: ### Step 5: Launch Wokwi Simulation
160: 1. Open `diagram.json` in the VS Code editor.
161: 2. Press `F1` (or `Ctrl + Shift + P`) to open the Command Palette.
162: 3. Run: **`Wokwi: Start Simulator`** (or click the green Play button).
163: 4. Watch the integrated Serial Monitor output:
164:    ```text
165:    --------------------------------------------------
166:      [PHASE 1 EXECUTION] Mounting MicroSD via VSPI   
167:    --------------------------------------------------
168:    [PHASE 1 SUCCESS] FAT32 Storage Mounted.
169:    [PHASE 1 CAPACITY] Total: 8 MB | Used: ...
170:    [PHASE 1 STORAGE] Seeded /www/index.html
171:    [PHASE 1 STORAGE] Seeded /lab_report.txt
172:    [PHASE 2 NET] Wi-Fi Connected!
173:    [PHASE 2 NET] Node IP Address: 10.13.37.2
174:    [PHASE 2 HTTP] Server active and listening on port 80.
175:    ```
176: 
177: ---
178: 
179: ## Simultaneous Multi-Interface Access (Ethernet LAN + Wi-Fi Hotspot)
180: 
181: ### Why Multi-Interface Works (0.0.0.0:9080 Binding)
182: When you start the gateway using:
183: ```powershell
184: .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
185: ```
186: The gateway binary does **not** bind strictly to `127.0.0.1`. Instead, it binds to socket `0.0.0.0:9080` (INADDR_ANY), meaning it actively listens on **every network interface enabled on your Windows host PC**.
187: 
188: This allows you to serve the simulated ESP32 NAS simultaneously across both wired and wireless networks!
189: 
190: ```
191:                        +---------------------------------------+
192:                        |   Host Workstation (0.0.0.0:9080)    |
193:                        |       wokwigw.exe TCP Forwarder       |
194:                        +-------------------+-------------------+
195:                                            |
196:                     +----------------------+----------------------+
197:                     |                                             |
198:                     ▼                                             ▼
199:        [Wired Ethernet Interface]                    [Windows Mobile Hotspot]
200:         IP: e.g. 192.168.1.105                         Virtual IP: 192.168.137.1
201:                     |                                             |
202:                     ▼                                             ▼
203:           Lab Desktop PCs on LAN                       Smartphones & Tablets
204:     http://192.168.1.105:9080/                      http://192.168.137.1:9080/
205: ```
206: 
207: ### Method A: Wireless Access via Windows Mobile Hotspot
208: To allow smartphones, tablets, and external laptops to connect wirelessly without lab router credentials:
209: 1. Open Windows **Settings > Network & internet > Mobile hotspot**.
210: 2. Select **Share my internet connection from**: `Ethernet` (or `Wi-Fi`).
211: 3. Set **Share over**: `Wi-Fi`.
212: 4. Turn **Mobile hotspot** to **ON**.
213: 5. Note your hotspot Network Name (SSID) and Password.
214: 6. Connect external smartphones or tablets to this hotspot.
215: 7. Windows automatically assigns the host PC an IP of **`192.168.137.1`** on the virtual hotspot adapter.
216: 8. On the connected phone/tablet, open any mobile browser and navigate to:
217:    - **`http://192.168.137.1:9080/`** (NAS Dashboard)
218:    - **`http://192.168.137.1:9080/site`** (Static Webpage)
219: 
220: ### Method B: Wired Access via Physical Ethernet LAN Switch
221: To allow lab PCs on the local campus network switch to access the node:
222: 1. Ensure your host machine is connected to the lab Ethernet switch/wall port.
223: 2. Open PowerShell and find your local Ethernet IPv4 address:
224:    ```powershell
225:    ipconfig
226:    ```
227:    *(Look for `IPv4 Address` under Ethernet adapter, e.g., `192.168.1.105` or `10.100.x.x`).*
228: 3. From any other lab desktop PC connected to the same switch/subnet, open the browser and navigate to:
229:    - **`http://<YOUR_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/`** (e.g. `http://192.168.1.105:9080/`)
230:    - **`http://<YOUR_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/site`**
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ### Endpoint & Host IP Mapping Table
235: 
236: Use this reference table to access the appropriate endpoints during your live lab evaluation:
237: 
238: | Interface Type | Connected Client Device | Host IP Reference | NAS Explorer URL | Hosted Static Site URL |
239: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
240: | **Localhost (Loopback)** | Host PC (Where VS Code is running) | `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` | [http://localhost:9080/](http://localhost:9080/) | [http://localhost:9080/site](http://localhost:9080/site) |
241: | **Windows Mobile Hotspot** | Evaluator smartphones, tablets, laptops | `192.168.137.1` *(Default Windows Hotspot Gateway)* | `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` | `http://192.168.137.1:9080/site` |
242: | **Wired Ethernet LAN** | Lab workstation PCs on campus switch | `<YOUR_LAN_IP>` *(From `ipconfig`)* | `http://<YOUR_LAN_IP>:9080/` | `http://<YOUR_LAN_IP>:9080/site` |
243: 
244: ---
245: 
246: ## Local Network File Sharing (LocalSend Web Model)
247: 
248: ### Workflow: Sharing Files Between Two Lab Computers
249: Just like the **"Share via Browser" (Web Share)** mode in **LocalSend**, `Project.MM` enables zero-installation local network file exchange between two lab computers or workstations via a standard web browser:
250: 
251: ```text
252:  [Lab PC 1: Host Node]                                 [Lab PC 2: Peer Client]
253:  +----------------------------------+                  +----------------------------------+
254:  | Wokwi Simulator (ESP32 DevKit)   |                  | Standard Web Browser             |
255:  |   ↕ (WS: ws://localhost:9011)    |                  | (Chrome / Edge / Firefox)        |
256:  | wokwigw.exe (0.0.0.0:9080)       |                  |                                  |
257:  | Windows Firewall Port 9080 OPEN  |                  | Navigates to:                    |
258:  +-----------------+----------------+                  | http://<PC1_IP>:9080/            |
259:                    |                                   +-----------------+----------------+
260:                    |                                                     |
261:                    +=================== LAN SWITCH =====================+
262:                                (or Windows Mobile Hotspot)
263: ```
264: 
265: 1. **Host Setup (PC 1)**: Runs the Wokwi simulation with `wokwigw.exe` and opens `http://localhost:9080/` (or `http://<PC1_IP>:9080/`).
266: 2. **Peer Connection (PC 2)**: Without installing any desktop apps, PC 2 opens its browser and navigates to `http://<PC1_IP>:9080/`.
267: 3. **Bi-directional Sharing**:
268:    - PC 1 uploads a file (e.g., `labtest2A.asm`) $\rightarrow$ Stored in the MicroSD FAT32 filesystem $\rightarrow$ PC 2 refreshes and clicks **Download**.
269:    - PC 2 selects a file (e.g., `lab_report.txt`) in the upload box $\rightarrow$ Uploads directly to the ESP32 storage $\rightarrow$ PC 1 refreshes and downloads it.
270: 4. **Real-Time Storage Telemetry**: Both computers see the dynamic storage capacity progress bar update in real-time as files are written and deleted.
271: 
272: ---
273: 
274: ### Architectural Comparison: Project.MM vs. LocalSend Web
275: 
276: While the front-end user experience mirrors LocalSend Web, the underlying embedded systems architecture fulfills the hardware requirements of `CSE0611324`:
277: 
278: | Dimension | LocalSend Web ("Share via Browser") | Project.MM Embedded NAS (`LocalConfig`) |
279: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
280: | **Compute Engine** | Heavy OS desktop application (Flutter / Rust / Dart on PC with 16 GB RAM) | **Classic ESP32 MCU** (Xtensa 32-bit Dual-Core LX6 @ 240 MHz, 520 KB SRAM) |
281: | **Storage Architecture** | Standard OS filesystem calls to PC NVMe/SSD drive | **Hardware VSPI Bus (SCK:18, MISO:19, MOSI:23, CS:5)** driving raw FAT32 SD block sectors |
282: | **Memory Budget** | Megabytes to gigabytes allocated in OS heap buffers | **Strict ~2 KB Streaming Window**: multipart upload chunks and download streams never overload SRAM |
283: | **Host Independence** | **Host-dependent**: If PC 1 closes the LocalSend window, sharing terminates immediately | **Independent Appliance**: The ESP32 is a standalone network node. Both PC 1 and PC 2 are equal clients connecting to external hardware |
284: | **Additional Services** | File transfer only | **Dual Service**: Simultaneous NAS file server + hosted static web node (`/site` streaming `/www/index.html` from SD card) |
285: 
286: ---
287: 
288: ### Lab Demonstration Checklist
289: 
290: 1. **Firewall Rule**: On PC 1, execute [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator.
291: 2. **Start Gateway**: In PowerShell, run:
292:    ```powershell
293:    .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
294:    ```
295: 3. **Start Simulation**: Open [`diagram.json`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/diagram.json), press `F1`, and select **`Wokwi: Start Simulator`**.
296: 4. **Find Host IP**: Run `ipconfig` on PC 1 to get its IPv4 address (e.g., `192.168.1.105` on LAN or `192.168.137.1` on Hotspot).
297: 5. **Access from PC 2**: Open browser on PC 2 and navigate to `http://<PC1_IP>:9080/`.
298: 6. **Exchange Files**: Upload from PC 1 $\rightarrow$ download from PC 2; upload from PC 2 $\rightarrow$ download from PC 1.
299: 
300: ---
301: 
302: ## Access Endpoints
303: 
304: Once `wokwigw` and the simulation are active, the web endpoints provide:
305: - **NAS File Manager Dashboard (`/`)**: Displays real-time FAT32 storage capacity meter, file list, file upload form, and file delete buttons.
306: - **Hosted Static Webpage (`/site`)**: Streams `/www/index.html` stored on the virtual MicroSD card.
307: - **Direct File Download (`/get?file=<name>`)**: Streams requested files in binary octet-stream mode directly to the client device.
308: - **Multipart Upload (`/upload`)**: Streams client files chunk-by-chunk into MicroSD FAT32 storage with ~2 KB RAM overhead.
309: 
310: ---
311: 
312: ## Troubleshooting & Tips
313: 
314: - **`connect tcp 10.13.37.2:80: no route to host` Error**:
315:   - **Cause**: The Wokwi simulator did not connect to `wokwigw`'s internal WebSocket server (`ws://localhost:9011`), meaning the virtual ESP32 is not registered in the gateway's network table.
316:   - **Fix**:
317:     1. Ensure `wokwi.toml` includes:
318:        ```toml
319:        [net]
320:        gateway = "ws://localhost:9011"
321:        ```
322:     2. **Start `wokwigw.exe` FIRST** in a separate terminal:
323:        ```powershell
324:        .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
325:        ```
326:     3. **Then Restart the Wokwi Simulation**: In VS Code, open `diagram.json`, press `F1`, and run `Wokwi: Restart Simulator` (or `Start Simulator`).
327:     4. In the `wokwigw` terminal, you should see confirmation of a connected client / DHCP lease.
328:     5. Wait until the Serial Monitor displays:
329:        ```text
330:        [WIFI] Connected!
331:        [NET] Node IP Address: 10.13.37.2
332:        ```
333:     6. Only now open `http://localhost:9080/` in your browser.
334: 
335: - **External Clients Cannot Connect (Connection Timed Out)**:
336:   - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator to verify Windows Firewall permits TCP port 9080 on Private and Public network profiles.
337: - **IP Mismatch**: The standard Wokwi gateway subnet is `10.13.37.2`. If your Serial Monitor displays a different node IP address, adjust the forwarding argument: `--forward 9080:<node-ip>:80`.

# Project.MM LocalConfig: Simulation & Network Execution Guide

An operational guide for compiling, running, and simulating the ESP32 Embedded Network Attached Storage (NAS) and Static Web Server within Visual Studio Code, and accessing the server from external client devices (smartphones, tablets, and peer lab computers) across local Wi-Fi and Ethernet networks.

---

## Table of Contents
- [1. System & Architecture Overview](#1-system--architecture-overview)
  - [1.1 Embedded Hardware Architecture](#11-embedded-hardware-architecture)
  - [1.2 Hardware VSPI & Storage Pinout](#12-hardware-vspi--storage-pinout)
  - [1.3 Zero-Overhead Streaming Architecture](#13-zero-overhead-streaming-architecture)
  - [1.4 Dual-Core FreeRTOS Task Separation](#14-dual-core-freertos-task-separation)
  - [1.5 Dual-Network Gateway Routing Model](#15-dual-network-gateway-routing-model)
- [2. Prerequisites & Extension Setup](#2-prerequisites--extension-setup)
  - [2.1 Required Software & Extensions](#21-required-software--extensions)
  - [2.2 Wokwi License Activation](#22-wokwi-license-activation)
  - [2.3 Opening the Workspace Correctly](#23-opening-the-workspace-correctly)
- [3. Step-by-Step Simulation Execution](#3-step-by-step-simulation-execution)
  - [Step 1: Compile Firmware via PlatformIO](#step-1-compile-firmware-via-platformio)
  - [Step 2: Configure Windows Firewall](#step-2-configure-windows-firewall)
  - [Step 3: Launch Local Network Gateway (wokwigw)](#step-3-launch-local-network-gateway-wokwigw)
  - [Step 4: Start Wokwi Simulation](#step-4-start-wokwi-simulation)
  - [Step 5: Verify Boot Telemetry in Serial Monitor](#step-5-verify-boot-telemetry-in-serial-monitor)
- [4. Accessing the Server from External Devices](#4-accessing-the-server-from-external-devices)
  - [4.1 Why Multi-Interface Access Works (0.0.0.0:9080 Binding)](#41-why-multi-interface-access-works-00009080-binding)
  - [4.2 Method A: Wireless Access via Windows Mobile Hotspot (Phones & Tablets)](#42-method-a-wireless-access-via-windows-mobile-hotspot-phones--tablets)
  - [4.3 Method B: Wired Access via Physical Ethernet LAN Switch (Lab Desktop PCs)](#43-method-b-wired-access-via-physical-ethernet-lan-switch-lab-desktop-pcs)
  - [4.4 Method C: Shared Campus / Home Wi-Fi Router](#44-method-c-shared-campus--home-wi-fi-router)
  - [4.5 Master Endpoint & Host IP Mapping Table](#45-master-endpoint--host-ip-mapping-table)
- [5. Zero-Install Local Network File Sharing (LocalSend Web Model)](#5-zero-install-local-network-file-sharing-localsend-web-model)
  - [5.1 Bi-Directional File Transfer Workflow](#51-bi-directional-file-transfer-workflow)
  - [5.2 Web Endpoints & Service Breakdown](#52-web-endpoints--service-breakdown)
- [6. Troubleshooting & Common Pitfalls](#6-troubleshooting--common-pitfalls)
  - [6.1 Error: connect tcp 10.13.37.2:80: no route to host](#61-error-connect-tcp-101337280-no-route-to-host)
  - [6.2 Connection Timed Out from External Devices](#62-connection-timed-out-from-external-devices)
  - [6.3 Wokwi Cannot Find Firmware Binary](#63-wokwi-cannot-find-firmware-binary)
  - [6.4 MicroSD Card Mount Failure](#64-microsd-card-mount-failure)
- [7. Quick-Reference Command Cheat Sheet](#7-quick-reference-command-cheat-sheet)

---

## 1. System & Architecture Overview

[`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) contains a fully self-contained local simulation setup for an **ESP32-based Embedded Network Attached Storage (NAS) and Static Web Server**. Designed for the `CSE0611324` Microprocessor & Microcontrollers laboratory curriculum, it runs completely on your workstation without cloud dependencies or upload rate limits.

```
                      +---------------------------------------------------+
                      |               Host Workstation                    |
                      |   VS Code + PlatformIO + Wokwi Simulator Engine   |
                      +-------------------------+-------------------------+
                                                |
                                    ws://localhost:9011
                                                |
                                                ▼
                                    +-----------------------+
                                    |     wokwigw.exe       |
                                    | (Listens: 0.0.0.0:9080)|
                                    +-----------+-----------+
                                                |
                         +----------------------+----------------------+
                         |                                             |
                         ▼                                             ▼
            [Wired Ethernet Interface]                    [Windows Mobile Hotspot]
             IP: e.g., 192.168.1.105                        Virtual IP: 192.168.137.1
                         |                                             |
                         ▼                                             ▼
            Lab Workstations / PCs                       Smartphones & Tablets
```

### 1.1 Embedded Hardware Architecture
* **Target Microcontroller**: Classic ESP32 DevKit V1 powered by the Xtensa Dual-Core 32-bit LX6 microprocessor operating at 240 MHz, with 520 KB on-chip SRAM.
* **Storage Medium**: Hardware VSPI-driven MicroSD Card module formatted with standard FAT32 block storage.
* **Firmware Framework**: Native Arduino-ESP32 core (`WebServer.h`, `SD.h`, `SPI.h`, `WiFi.h`).

### 1.2 Hardware VSPI & Storage Pinout
The storage subsystem directly interfaces with the ESP32 hardware VSPI bus via physical GPIO pins defined in [`src/main.cpp`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp) and [`diagram.json`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/diagram.json):

| ESP32 Hardware Pin | Signal Function | MicroSD Module Pin | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`GPIO 5`** | **`CS`** (SS) | `CS` | Chip Select (Active Low) |
| **`GPIO 18`** | **`SCK`** | `SCK` / `CLK` | Serial Clock |
| **`GPIO 23`** | **`MOSI`** | `DI` | Master Out Slave In |
| **`GPIO 19`** | **`MISO`** | `DO` | Master In Slave Out |
| **`3V3`** | **`VCC`** | `VCC` | 3.3V Regulated Power |
| **`GND`** | **`GND`** | `GND` | Ground Reference |

### 1.3 Zero-Overhead Streaming Architecture
To prevent SRAM exhaustion on the 520 KB microcontroller during multi-megabyte file transfers:
* **Uploads**: Handled via `server.upload()` chunk-by-chunk streaming directly to the SD filesystem.
* **Downloads**: Handled via `server.streamFile()` in binary chunk buffers.
* **RAM Footprint**: Fixed at approximately **~2 KB** of heap memory regardless of whether transferring a 10 KB assembly program or a 20 MB binary image.

### 1.4 Dual-Core FreeRTOS Task Separation
The ESP32 firmware leverages dual-core Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP):
* **Core 0**: Dedicated strictly to the lwIP (Lightweight IP) TCP/IP protocol stack and asynchronous Wi-Fi driver packet handling.
* **Core 1**: Runs the primary application event loop (`server.handleClient()`), SD card FAT32 sector reads/writes, and automated self-diagnostic health checks pinned via `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`.

### 1.5 Dual-Network Gateway Routing Model
Virtual Wi-Fi inside the Wokwi simulator uses a private virtual subnet (`10.13.37.2`). The companion bridge binary [`wokwigw.exe`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwigw.exe) bridges this virtual subnet to the host:
* Communicates with Wokwi over WebSocket on `ws://localhost:9011`.
* Forwards host port `9080` to virtual ESP32 port `80` via:
  ```powershell
  .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
  ```
* Binds to `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`), making the simulator reachable over **Localhost**, **Physical Ethernet LAN**, and **Windows Mobile Hotspot Wi-Fi** at the same time.

---

## 2. Prerequisites & Extension Setup

### 2.1 Required Software & Extensions
Ensure your workstation has the following installed:
1. **Visual Studio Code** (version 1.80+ recommended).
2. **PlatformIO IDE Extension** (`platformio.platformio-ide`):
   - Handles the GCC Xtensa compiler toolchain, Arduino-ESP32 core libraries, and binary compilation.
3. **Wokwi Simulator Extension** (`wokwi.wokwi-vscode`):
   - Provides cycle-accurate hardware simulation and virtual SPI/Wi-Fi peripherals.

### 2.2 Wokwi License Activation
If this is your first time using the Wokwi extension in VS Code:
1. Press `F1` (or `Ctrl + Shift + P`) to open the Command Palette.
2. Type and select **`Wokwi: Request License`**.
3. Follow the one-time browser verification link to claim your license.

### 2.3 Opening the Workspace Correctly
> [!IMPORTANT]
> To prevent path mismatch errors, open the directory [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) directly in VS Code (`File` > `Open Folder...`).
>
> If you open the top-level repository root (`Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab`), you must tell Wokwi where to find the configuration:
> 1. Press `F1` $\rightarrow$ select **`Wokwi: Select Config File`**.
> 2. Pick [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml).

---

## 3. Step-by-Step Simulation Execution

Follow these steps in exact order to launch the simulation successfully:

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Step 1: Compile Firmware (PlatformIO Build: Ctrl + Alt + B)                      |
|                                     ▼                                             |
|  Step 2: Configure Windows Firewall (Run setup_firewall.bat as Admin)              |
|                                     ▼                                             |
|  Step 3: Launch Gateway Terminal (.\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80)     |
|                                     ▼                                             |
|  Step 4: Launch Wokwi Simulation (diagram.json -> Wokwi: Start Simulator)         |
|                                     ▼                                             |
|  Step 5: Verify Serial Output & Access http://localhost:9080/                      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Step 1: Compile Firmware via PlatformIO
1. Open the project in VS Code.
2. Compile the C++ firmware into a simulation binary using any of these methods:
   - Click the **Build Checkmark (✓)** icon on the bottom blue status bar.
   - Press the keyboard shortcut `Ctrl + Alt + B`.
   - Open the VS Code integrated terminal and run:
     ```powershell
     pio run
     ```
3. PlatformIO will download the required `espressif32` platform tools and compile the binary to:
   ```text
   .pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin
   ```

### Step 2: Configure Windows Firewall
External devices connecting to your PC's IP on port `9080` will be blocked by Windows Firewall by default. To whitelist port `9080`:
1. In File Explorer or inside the VS Code terminal, locate [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat).
2. Right-click and choose **Run as administrator** (or double-click; it auto-elevates via UAC).
3. The script executes the following PowerShell rule across all network profiles (Domain, Private, Public):
   ```powershell
   New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Wokwi Gateway NAS" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 9080 -Protocol TCP -Profile Any -Action Allow
   ```
4. Verify the terminal prints:
   ```text
   [SUCCESS] Port 9080 is now open across all profiles!
   ```

### Step 3: Launch Local Network Gateway (wokwigw)
The gateway must be running **before** starting the simulation so the ESP32 can register on the virtual network:
1. Open a new PowerShell terminal in VS Code (`Ctrl + Shift + \``).
2. Navigate to the `LocalConfig` folder:
   ```powershell
   cd d:\GitHub\UITS\Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab\Project.MM\LocalConfig
   ```
3. Start the forwarder:
   ```powershell
   .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
   ```
4. You will see output confirming the listener has started:
   ```text
   wokwigw version 0.1.0
   Listening on 0.0.0.0:9080 -> 10.13.37.2:80
   WebSocket server listening on ws://127.0.0.1:9011
   ```
5. **Keep this terminal window open and running.** Do not close it.

### Step 4: Start Wokwi Simulation
1. Click to open [`diagram.json`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/diagram.json) in VS Code editor.
2. Press `F1` (or `Ctrl + Shift + P`) to open the Command Palette.
3. Type and select: **`Wokwi: Start Simulator`** (or click the green **Play** button at the top of the diagram view).

### Step 5: Verify Boot Telemetry in Serial Monitor
Observe the integrated Serial Monitor window in VS Code. You should see the complete boot sequence:
```text
--------------------------------------------------
  [PHASE 1 EXECUTION] Mounting MicroSD via VSPI   
--------------------------------------------------
[PHASE 1 SUCCESS] FAT32 Storage Mounted.
[PHASE 1 CAPACITY] Total: 8 MB | Used: 1 MB
[STORAGE] Seeded modern /www/index.html to SD
[STORAGE] Seeded /lab_report.txt to SD
[PHASE 1 DIRECTORY TREE]:
  |- /www (DIR)
  |- /www/index.html (3.4 KB)
  |- /lab_report.txt (240 B)
--------------------------------------------------

[PHASE 2 NET] Connecting to Wi-Fi SSID: Wokwi-GUEST ...
[PHASE 2 NET] Wi-Fi Connected!
[PHASE 2 NET] Node IP Address: 10.13.37.2
[PHASE 2 HTTP] Server active and listening on port 80.
[PHASE 2 ENDPOINTS]
  - NAS Explorer : http://10.13.37.2/
  - Static Web   : http://10.13.37.2/site
  - File Download: http://10.13.37.2/get?file=<name>
  - File Upload  : http://10.13.37.2/upload (POST)
  - File Delete  : http://10.13.37.2/delete?file=<name>
```

Open your host browser to test local access:
* **NAS Dashboard**: [http://localhost:9080/](http://localhost:9080/)
* **Static Hosted Website**: [http://localhost:9080/site](http://localhost:9080/site)

---

## 4. Accessing the Server from External Devices

You can connect external smartphones, tablets, and peer lab PCs to the simulated ESP32 without modifying any simulation files.

### 4.1 Why Multi-Interface Access Works (0.0.0.0:9080 Binding)
When `wokwigw.exe` starts, it creates a socket listening on `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`). Rather than locking to loopback (`127.0.0.1`), it accepts incoming TCP packets on **every physical and virtual network adapter** active on the Windows host machine.

Any device that can ping or route to an IP address belonging to your host PC can access the ESP32 server over port `9080`.

---

### 4.2 Method A: Wireless Access via Windows Mobile Hotspot (Phones & Tablets)
This method is ideal when you want evaluators, instructors, or lab partners to access the server from their smartphones or laptops without needing lab router passwords.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Host PC (Windows 10 / 11)                                                        |
|  1. Enable Windows Mobile Hotspot (Share over: Wi-Fi)                             |
|  2. Windows assigns Host Virtual IP: 192.168.137.1                                |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                          ▲
                                          │ (Wi-Fi Connection)
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Client Smartphone / Tablet                                                       |
|  1. Connect Wi-Fi to Host Hotspot SSID                                            |
|  2. Open Mobile Browser -> http://192.168.137.1:9080/                             |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

#### Step-by-Step Instructions:
1. **Enable Hotspot on Host PC**:
   - Open Windows **Settings** (`Win + I`) $\rightarrow$ **Network & internet** $\rightarrow$ **Mobile hotspot**.
   - Set **Share my internet connection from**: `Ethernet` (or `Wi-Fi`).
   - Set **Share over**: `Wi-Fi`.
   - Toggle **Mobile hotspot** to **ON**.
   - Note the **Network name (SSID)** and **Network password**.
2. **Deterministic Hotspot IP**:
   - Windows automatically assigns the host PC a fixed gateway IP of **`192.168.137.1`** on the virtual hotspot adapter.
3. **Connect Client Device**:
   - On your phone or tablet, go to Wi-Fi settings and connect to the host PC's hotspot SSID.
4. **Browse Endpoints**:
   - Open Chrome, Safari, or Firefox on the phone and navigate to:
     - **NAS Dashboard**: `http://192.168.137.1:9080/`
     - **Static Site**: `http://192.168.137.1:9080/site`
5. **Interactive Verification**:
   - Take a photo on your phone and upload it via the browser dashboard. Watch the file appear instantly in the storage table and in the VS Code Serial Monitor!

---

### 4.3 Method B: Wired Access via Physical Ethernet LAN Switch (Lab Desktop PCs)
Use this method to share files directly with neighboring desktop PCs connected to the same campus lab switch or router.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Lab PC 1 (Host Node Running Simulation)                                          |
|  1. Connected to Ethernet Switch                                                  |
|  2. Find Ethernet IPv4 via 'ipconfig' (e.g., 192.168.1.105)                       |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                          ▲
                                          │ (Physical Ethernet LAN Switch)
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Lab PC 2 (Peer Client Desktop)                                                   |
|  1. Connected to Same Lab Ethernet Switch                                         |
|  2. Open Browser -> http://192.168.1.105:9080/                                    |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

#### Step-by-Step Instructions:
1. **Verify Host Network Connection**:
   - Ensure the host PC is connected via Ethernet cable to the lab switch.
2. **Find Host LAN IP Address**:
   - On the host PC, open PowerShell and run:
     ```powershell
     ipconfig
     ```
   - Look for the section labeled **Ethernet adapter Ethernet** and note the **IPv4 Address**:
     ```text
     Ethernet adapter Ethernet:
        IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.105
        Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
        Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.1
     ```
3. **Connect from Peer Lab PC**:
   - Go to any other desktop computer in the lab connected to the same network.
   - Open any browser and navigate to:
     - `http://<HOST_IP>:9080/` (e.g., `http://192.168.1.105:9080/`)
     - `http://<HOST_IP>:9080/site`

---

### 4.4 Method C: Shared Campus / Home Wi-Fi Router
If both your host laptop and client devices are connected to the same wireless router:
1. Open PowerShell on the host laptop and run `ipconfig`.
2. Look under **Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi** for your IPv4 address (e.g., `192.168.0.45` or `10.100.x.x`).
3. On any client device on the same Wi-Fi, open the browser and enter:
   ```text
   http://192.168.0.45:9080/
   ```

> [!NOTE]
> On public campus networks with "Client Isolation" (AP Isolation) enabled, Wi-Fi devices may be prevented from talking directly to each other. If you encounter this, switch immediately to **Method A (Windows Mobile Hotspot)**, which bypasses router restrictions entirely.

### 4.5 Master Endpoint & Host IP Mapping Table

| Interface Type | Connected Client Device | Host IP Used in URL | NAS Dashboard URL | Static Hosted Web URL |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Localhost (Loopback)** | Host PC (where VS Code is running) | `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` | [http://localhost:9080/](http://localhost:9080/) | [http://localhost:9080/site](http://localhost:9080/site) |
| **Windows Mobile Hotspot** | External phones, tablets, laptops | `192.168.137.1` *(Default)* | `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` | `http://192.168.137.1:9080/site` |
| **Physical Ethernet LAN** | Lab desktop PCs on campus switch | `<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>` *(from `ipconfig`)* | `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/` | `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/site` |
| **Standard Wi-Fi LAN** | Laptops/phones on shared home/office Wi-Fi | `<HOST_WIFI_IP>` *(from `ipconfig`)* | `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/` | `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/site` |

## 5. Zero-Install Local Network File Sharing (LocalSend Web Model)

### 5.1 Bi-Directional File Transfer Workflow
`Project.MM` functions identically to the popular **LocalSend "Share via Browser"** web feature. No software or apps need to be installed on client devices:

```text
  [Lab PC 1: Host Node]                                 [Lab PC 2: Peer Client]
  +----------------------------------+                  +----------------------------------+
  | Wokwi Simulator (ESP32 DevKit)   |                  | Standard Web Browser             |
  |   ↕ (ws://localhost:9011)        |                  | (Chrome / Edge / Safari)         |
  | wokwigw.exe (0.0.0.0:9080)       |                  |                                  |
  | Windows Firewall Port 9080 OPEN  |                  | Navigates to:                    |
  +-----------------+----------------+                  | http://<HOST_IP>:9080/           |
                    |                                   +-----------------+----------------+
                    |                                                     |
                    +=================== LAN SWITCH =====================+
                                (or Windows Mobile Hotspot)
```

1. **Step A (Upload from PC 1 $\rightarrow$ Download on PC 2)**:
   - On PC 1, go to `http://localhost:9080/` and upload an assembly file (e.g., `labtest2.asm`).
   - The file is written to the virtual MicroSD card.
   - On PC 2, refresh `http://<HOST_IP>:9080/` and click the **Download** button. The file streams directly from the ESP32 storage into PC 2's Downloads folder.
2. **Step B (Upload from PC 2 $\rightarrow$ Download on PC 1)**:
   - On PC 2, click **Choose File**, select a report (e.g., `report.pdf`), and click **Upload to ESP32**.
   - On PC 1, refresh the dashboard to see `report.pdf` listed and download it locally.
3. **Step C (Live Storage Telemetry)**:
   - As files are uploaded or deleted, the dynamic storage progress bar automatically updates the total capacity, used space, and free space in real-time.

---

### 5.2 Web Endpoints & Service Breakdown

The ESP32 firmware in [`src/main.cpp`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp) serves five dedicated REST/HTTP routes:

* **`GET /` (NAS Dashboard)**:
  - Generates the responsive glassmorphic dark-theme UI defined in [`include/html_templates.h`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/include/html_templates.h).
  - Displays hardware telemetry (CPU frequency, chip model, free heap, storage usage) and the active file directory table.
* **`GET /site` (Static Web Hosting)**:
  - Streams the pre-seeded static webpage `/www/index.html` stored on the MicroSD card directly to the client browser.
* **`GET /get?file=<filename>` (File Download)**:
  - Streams any file on the FAT32 filesystem as a `binary/octet-stream` download attachment.
* **`POST /upload` (Multipart File Upload)**:
  - Receives multi-part file payloads and streams them directly into `SD.open(filename, FILE_WRITE)` using a fixed ~2 KB buffer.
* **`GET /delete?file=<filename>` (File Removal)**:
  - Deletes the specified file from the SD card using `SD.remove()` and redirects back to `/`.

---

## 6. Troubleshooting & Common Pitfalls

### 6.1 Error: `connect tcp 10.13.37.2:80: no route to host`
* **Root Cause**: The Wokwi simulator was started before `wokwigw.exe`, or Wokwi failed to connect to `ws://localhost:9011`. The virtual ESP32 is therefore not registered in the gateway's routing table.
* **Solution**:
  1. Verify [`wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml) includes:
     ```toml
     [net]
     gateway = "ws://localhost:9011"
     ```
  2. Stop the Wokwi simulation in VS Code (click the Stop icon in the diagram).
  3. Ensure `wokwigw.exe` is actively running in its own terminal window:
     ```powershell
     .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
     ```
  4. Now restart the simulator: open [`diagram.json`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/diagram.json), press `F1`, and select **`Wokwi: Start Simulator`**.
  5. The `wokwigw` terminal will log `New connection from 127.0.0.1` and assign DHCP IP `10.13.37.2`.

---

### 6.2 Connection Timed Out from External Devices
* **Root Cause 1: Windows Firewall Blocking Port 9080**:
  - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator to add the inbound rule for TCP port 9080.
* **Root Cause 2: Wrong IPv4 Address**:
  - Re-run `ipconfig` on the host machine to make sure your IP has not changed after switching networks.
* **Root Cause 3: AP / Client Isolation on Campus Wi-Fi**:
  - Public institutional Wi-Fi networks frequently block peer-to-peer traffic. Switch to **Method A (Windows Mobile Hotspot)** so your laptop acts as the router.

---

### 6.3 Wokwi Cannot Find Firmware Binary
* **Root Cause**: The project has not been compiled yet, or the workspace was opened at a different folder level.
* **Solution**:
  1. Run `pio run` (or press `Ctrl + Alt + B`) to verify `.pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin` is generated.
  2. If opened from the repository root, press `F1` $\rightarrow$ select **`Wokwi: Select Config File`** $\rightarrow$ choose [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml).

---

### 6.4 MicroSD Card Mount Failure
* **Root Cause**: Wiring mismatch in simulation schematics.
* **Solution**: Inspect [`diagram.json`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/diagram.json) to verify the VSPI pin assignments:
  - `esp:D5` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:CS`
  - `esp:D18` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:SCK`
  - `esp:D19` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:DO`
  - `esp:D23` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:DI`

---

---

## 3. Analysis & Architectural Insights

### 3.1 Hardware VSPI & Streaming Constraints
The simulated system models an ESP32 microcontroller with 520 KB on-chip SRAM communicating with a MicroSD card over the hardware VSPI bus (`SCK:18`, `MISO:19`, `MOSI:23`, `CS:5`). To prevent Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes during large file transfers between lab machines:
* Uploads are streamed incrementally chunk-by-chunk using `server.upload()`.
* Downloads use binary chunked streaming via `server.streamFile()`.
* Total SRAM usage remains constrained at **~2 KB** regardless of file size.

### 3.2 Multi-Interface Socket Routing (0.0.0.0:9080)
The local companion forwarder `wokwigw.exe` binds to `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`), which instructs the Windows TCP/IP stack to accept incoming packets across all local interfaces:
1. **Loopback Adapter (`127.0.0.1` / `localhost:9080`)**: For browser testing on the host PC.
2. **Windows Mobile Hotspot (`192.168.137.1:9080`)**: Provides a deterministic gateway IP that bypasses campus network isolation, allowing smartphones and tablets to connect over Wi-Fi directly to the host PC.
3. **Physical Ethernet LAN (`<LAN_IP>:9080`)**: Enables neighboring desktop PCs plugged into the same lab Ethernet switch to access the node directly.

### 3.3 Windows Firewall & Virtual Subnet Gateway Bridging
The Wokwi simulation runs the ESP32 on a private virtual subnet (`10.13.37.2`). `wokwigw.exe` communicates with Wokwi over `ws://localhost:9011` and forwards TCP port 9080 to `10.13.37.2:80`. Because Windows blocks incoming connections on non-standard ports by default, [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) configures an inbound firewall rule (`Wokwi Gateway NAS`) across Domain, Private, and Public profiles to guarantee reliable zero-timeout connectivity.

1. **Clickable Table of Contents** adhering to GitHub Flavored Markdown navigation.

3. **Step-by-Step Execution Sequence**:

   - One-click Windows Firewall rule setup (`setup_firewall.bat`).
   - Gateway invocation (`wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80`).
   - Wokwi simulation launch (`diagram.json`).
   - Serial Monitor boot verification.
4. **Three Real-World Multi-Device Access Methods**:
   - Windows Mobile Hotspot Wi-Fi (`http://192.168.137.1:9080/`).
   - Campus Physical Ethernet LAN Switch (`http://<HOST_IP>:9080/`).
   - Shared Wi-Fi Router (`http://<HOST_IP>:9080/`).
5. **Local Network File Sharing Workflow (LocalSend Web Model)** illustrating zero-app file transfers between peer lab computers.
6. **Detailed Troubleshooting Section** resolving `no route to host`, firewall timeouts, missing binaries, and SD mount failures.
7. **Quick-Reference Cheat Sheet** summarizing all commands and URLs.

238: ## 4. Accessing the Server from External Devices
239: 
240: You can connect external smartphones, tablets, and peer lab PCs to the simulated ESP32 without modifying any simulation files.
241: 
242: ### 4.1 Why Multi-Interface Access Works (0.0.0.0:9080 Binding)
243: When `wokwigw.exe` starts, it creates a socket listening on `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`). Rather than locking to loopback (`127.0.0.1`), it accepts incoming TCP packets on **every physical and virtual network adapter** active on the Windows host machine.
244: 
245: Any device that can ping or route to an IP address belonging to your host PC can access the ESP32 server over port `9080`.
246: 
247: ---
248: 
249: ### 4.2 Method A: Wireless Access via Windows Mobile Hotspot (Phones & Tablets)
250: This method is ideal when you want evaluators, instructors, or lab partners to access the server from their smartphones or laptops without needing lab router passwords.
251: 
252: ```
253: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
254: |  Host PC (Windows 10 / 11)                                                        |
255: |  1. Enable Windows Mobile Hotspot (Share over: Wi-Fi)                             |
256: |  2. Windows assigns Host Virtual IP: 192.168.137.1                                |
257: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
258:                                           ▲
259:                                           │ (Wi-Fi Connection)
260: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
261: |  Client Smartphone / Tablet                                                       |
262: |  1. Connect Wi-Fi to Host Hotspot SSID                                            |
263: |  2. Open Mobile Browser -> http://192.168.137.1:9080/                             |
264: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
265: ```
266: 
267: #### Step-by-Step Instructions:
268: 1. **Enable Hotspot on Host PC**:
269:    - Open Windows **Settings** (`Win + I`) $\rightarrow$ **Network & internet** $\rightarrow$ **Mobile hotspot**.
270:    - Set **Share my internet connection from**: `Ethernet` (or `Wi-Fi`).
271:    - Set **Share over**: `Wi-Fi`.
272:    - Toggle **Mobile hotspot** to **ON**.
273:    - Note the **Network name (SSID)** and **Network password**.

275:    - Windows automatically assigns the host PC a fixed gateway IP of **`192.168.137.1`** on the virtual hotspot adapter.
276: 3. **Connect Client Device**:
277:    - On your phone or tablet, go to Wi-Fi settings and connect to the host PC's hotspot SSID.
278: 4. **Browse Endpoints**:

280:      - **NAS Dashboard**: `http://192.168.137.1:9080/`
281:      - **Static Site**: `http://192.168.137.1:9080/site`

47: ## 3. Analysis & Architectural Insights
48: 
49: ### 3.1 Hardware VSPI & Streaming Constraints
50: The simulated system models an ESP32 microcontroller with 520 KB on-chip SRAM communicating with a MicroSD card over the hardware VSPI bus (`SCK:18`, `MISO:19`, `MOSI:23`, `CS:5`). To prevent Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes during large file transfers between lab machines:
51: * Uploads are streamed incrementally chunk-by-chunk using `server.upload()`.
52: * Downloads use binary chunked streaming via `server.streamFile()`.
53: * Total SRAM usage remains constrained at **~2 KB** regardless of file size.
54: 
55: ### 3.2 Multi-Interface Socket Routing (0.0.0.0:9080)
56: The local companion forwarder `wokwigw.exe` binds to `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`), which instructs the Windows TCP/IP stack to accept incoming packets across all local interfaces:
57: 1. **Loopback Adapter (`127.0.0.1` / `localhost:9080`)**: For browser testing on the host PC.
58: 2. **Windows Mobile Hotspot (`192.168.137.1:9080`)**: Provides a deterministic gateway IP that bypasses campus network isolation, allowing smartphones and tablets to connect over Wi-Fi directly to the host PC.
59: 3. **Physical Ethernet LAN (`<LAN_IP>:9080`)**: Enables neighboring desktop PCs plugged into the same lab Ethernet switch to access the node directly.
60: 
61: ### 3.3 Windows Firewall & Virtual Subnet Gateway Bridging
62: The Wokwi simulation runs the ESP32 on a private virtual subnet (`10.13.37.2`). `wokwigw.exe` communicates with Wokwi over `ws://localhost:9011` and forwards TCP port 9080 to `10.13.37.2:80`. Because Windows blocks incoming connections on non-standard ports by default, [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) configures an inbound firewall rule (`Wokwi Gateway NAS`) across Domain, Private, and Public profiles to guarantee reliable zero-timeout connectivity.

---

### Scenario Breakdown & How Each Works

#### 1. Home Testing: Host on Ethernet $\leftrightarrow$ Client Device on Wi-Fi
* **How it works**: Standard home Wi-Fi routers bridge the physical Ethernet LAN ports and the wireless (2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi) radios into the exact same local broadcast subnet (typically `192.168.0.x` or `192.168.1.x`).
* **Which IP to use**: Because the host PC is communicating through its wired network card, run `ipconfig` on the host PC and find the **`IPv4 Address`** under **`Ethernet adapter Ethernet`** (e.g., `192.168.0.105`).
  > **Note**: Do **not** look for "Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi" on the host PC when it is plugged in via Ethernet; use the host's wired Ethernet IP.
* **On your client phone/laptop (connected to home Wi-Fi)**:
  - NAS File Dashboard: `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/` (e.g., `http://192.168.0.105:9080/`)
  - Static Webpage: `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/site`

---

#### 2. Lab Evaluation: Both Devices Connected via Campus Ethernet Switch
* **How it works**: Both your host PC (running the simulation) and the evaluator/peer lab PC are connected via RJ45 cables to the campus lab Ethernet switch on the same campus subnet (e.g. `10.100.x.x` or `192.168.1.x`).
* **Which IP to use**: Find the host's Ethernet IP via `ipconfig` (e.g., `10.100.22.45`).
* **On the peer lab PC**:
  - Open Chrome/Edge and browse to `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/`.
  - Zero software installation required on the peer PC—it operates on the **LocalSend Web** model directly in the browser.

---

#### 3. Portable Showcase & Defense: Laptop Mobile Hotspot (Phones & Tablets)
* **How it works**: When demonstrating to evaluators or if campus Wi-Fi has strict "AP/Client Isolation" blocking device-to-device communication, turn on **Windows Mobile Hotspot** on your laptop (`Win + I` $\rightarrow$ *Network & internet* $\rightarrow$ *Mobile hotspot* $\rightarrow$ *ON*).
* **Deterministic Gateway IP**:
  - Windows automatically assigns your host laptop the virtual IP **`192.168.137.1`** on the virtual hotspot adapter.
* **On any evaluator's or peer's phone/tablet**:
  - Connect to your laptop's hotspot Wi-Fi.
  - Browse to:
    - **`http://192.168.137.1:9080/`**
    - **`http://192.168.137.1:9080/site`**
* **Advantage**: 100% self-contained private wireless network, entirely independent of lab routers, campus firewalls, or internet connectivity.

28: ## 1. Overview
29: This setup guide provides all instructions, dependencies, and automated helper scripts needed to compile, simulate, and interact with the **ESP32 Embedded NAS & Static Web Node** locally on your workstation.
30: 
31: All simulation runs locally using:
32: - **PlatformIO**: C++ Espressif toolchain and Arduino framework compilation.
33: - **Wokwi Simulator for VS Code**: QEMU/Wasm virtual ESP32 DevKit and MicroSD module emulation.
34: - **Wokwi IoT Gateway (`wokwigw`)**: Local TCP bridge mapping `0.0.0.0:9080` (all host network interfaces) to virtual Wi-Fi `10.13.37.2:80`.
35: 
36: ---

39:

43: | **Python** | 3.10+ (tested on 3.14) | Executes PlatformIO build system |
44: | **Wokwi VS Code Extension** | Latest (`wokwi.wokwi-vscode`) | Hardware circuit simulation |
45: | **Wokwi IoT Gateway** | Standalone binary (`wokwigw.exe`) | Bridges browser to virtual Wi-Fi |
46:

49: ## 3. Automated One-Click Setup
50: 
51: Inside the `setup/` directory, automated script pairs (`.bat` and `.ps1`) manage the entire environment:

56: ### Step 0: Python Installation (For New / Fresh Devices)
57: If a device has not installed Python yet, run the automated Python installer:
58: ```cmd
59: .\Project.MM\setup\setup_python.bat
60: ```
61: *Or via PowerShell:*
62: ```powershell
63: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\Project.MM\setup\setup_python.ps1
64: ```
65: *What this does:*
66: 1. Checks if Python 3 is already installed and in PATH.
67: 2. If missing, attempts silent installation via `winget` (Windows Package Manager).
68: 3. If `winget` is unavailable, automatically downloads and silently runs the official Python 64-bit installer with `Add Python to PATH` enabled.
69: 4. Refreshes the environment variables so Python is immediately ready.
70: *(Note: `install_dependencies.bat` will also detect missing Python and invoke this automatically if needed!)*
71: 
72: ### Step 1: Verify & Install Dependencies
73: Run via **Batch Launcher** (Bypasses execution policy restrictions automatically):
74: ```cmd
75: .\Project.MM\setup\install_dependencies.bat
76: ```

78: ```powershell
79: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\Project.MM\setup\install_dependencies.ps1
80: ```
81: *What this does:*
82: 1. Verifies Python availability (and triggers automated setup if missing).
83: 2. Installs/updates PlatformIO CLI via pip.

85: 4. Checks for `wokwigw.exe` and ensures it is present in both `setup/` and `LocalConfig/`.
86: 5. Pre-installs Espressif 32 toolchains and framework packages with live download progress bars so subsequent builds execute in seconds.

33: 
34: ## Overview
35: This project sets up, compiles, simulates, and serves an ESP32-based Network Attached Storage (NAS) and Static Web Server entirely on your local workstation using the **Wokwi for VS Code** extension and **PlatformIO IDE**.
36: 
37: By running simulation locally, the ESP32 code executes via your local compiler toolchain without cloud rate limits, and network requests can be bridged directly to your host PC loopback adapter (`localhost:9080`) as well as external network interfaces (wired Ethernet and wireless Mobile Hotspot).
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## Project Directory Structure
42: 
43: ```text
44: Project.MM/LocalConfig/
45: │
46: ├── .gitignore             # Ignores .pio/ build artifacts and local IDE files
47: ├── platformio.ini         # Toolchain & dependency configuration
48: ├── wokwi.toml             # Wokwi simulation descriptor
49: ├── diagram.json           # Circuit schematics and SPI pin mappings
50: ├── wokwigw.exe            # Local network gateway binary
51: ├── setup_firewall.bat     # One-click UAC auto-elevated Windows Firewall rule installer
52: ├── README.md              # Project documentation and execution instructions
53: ├── include/
54: │   └── html_templates.h   # Modular glassmorphic HTML/CSS templates & PROGMEM strings
55: └── src/
56:     └── main.cpp           # ESP32 C++ firmware code
57: ```
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## Prerequisites & Extension Setup
62: 
63: 1. **Install Visual Studio Code**: Ensure VS Code is installed.
64: 2. **Install Extensions**:
65:    - Open VS Code Extensions view (`Ctrl + Shift + X`).
66:    - Search for and install **Wokwi Simulator** (`wokwi.wokwi-vscode`).
67:    - Search for and install **PlatformIO IDE** (`platformio.platformio-ide`).
68: 3. *(Optional for first-time Wokwi setup)*: Press `F1`, type `Wokwi: Request License`, and claim your free trial/license token if prompted by the extension.
69: 
70: ---
71: 
72: ## Configuration Files Breakdown
73: 
74: ### 1. `platformio.ini`
75: Instructs PlatformIO to compile firmware targeting the standard ESP32 DevKit using the Arduino framework:
76: ```ini
77: [env:esp32dev]
78: platform = espressif32
79: board = esp32dev
80: framework = arduino
81: monitor_speed = 115200
82: 
83: ; Built-in libraries used directly: WiFi, WebServer, SPI, SD, FS
84: lib_deps =
85: ```
86: 
87: ### 2. `wokwi.toml`
88: Tells Wokwi where PlatformIO places the compiled binary and ELF debug symbols, and routes simulation network traffic through the local `wokwigw` gateway:
89: ```toml
90: [wokwi]
91: version = 1
92: firmware = ".pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin"
93: elf = ".pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.elf"
94: 
95: [net]
96: gateway = "ws://localhost:9011"
97: ```
98: *(The `[net]` block is required for `wokwigw` so that virtual Wi-Fi packets are forwarded through the local gateway at `localhost:9011`).*
99: 
100: 
101: ### 3. `diagram.json`
102: Specifies virtual hardware and hardware SPI wiring (using Wokwi `D`-prefixed silkscreen pin names):
103: - **`wokwi-esp32-devkit-v1`**: Core MCU board.
104: - **`wokwi-microsd-card`**: SPI MicroSD card module.
105: - **Pin Connections**:
106:   - `esp:3V3` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:VCC`
107:   - `esp:GND.1` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:GND`
108:   - `esp:D5` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:CS` (Chip Select)
109:   - `esp:D23` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:DI` (MOSI)
110:   - `esp:D19` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:DO` (MISO)
111:   - `esp:D18` $\rightarrow$ `sd1:SCK` (Serial Clock)
112: 
113: ### 4. `include/html_templates.h`
114: Modular UI templates:
115: - Contains glassmorphic dark UI CSS styles, responsive layouts, storage bar templates, and the static website template (`SEED_INDEX_HTML`).
116: - Stored directly in Flash ROM using `PROGMEM` and C++ raw string literals `R"rawliteral(...)rawliteral"`, keeping internal SRAM free.
117: 
118: ### 5. `src/main.cpp`
119: Firmware architecture:
120: - **Phase 1 Storage**: Explicitly initializes `SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, 5)` and mounts FAT32 SD filesystem via `SD.begin(5, SPI)`. Automatically seeds `/www/index.html` and `/lab_report.txt` and enumerates files.
121: - **Phase 2 Networking**: Connects to `Wokwi-GUEST` Wi-Fi, hosts web endpoints on port 80 (`/`, `/site`, `/get`, `/upload`, `/delete`), and executes automated internal self-diagnostics on FreeRTOS Core 1.
122: 
123: ### 6. `setup_firewall.bat`
124: Automated administrative script:
125: - Automatically requests UAC elevation if not launched as Administrator.
126: - Executes `New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Wokwi Gateway NAS" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 9080 -Protocol TCP -Profile Any -Action Allow` to permit inbound traffic on port 9080 across all network profiles (Domain, Private, Public).
127: - Guarantees wired Ethernet LAN peers and wireless Mobile Hotspot devices can access the server without connection timeouts.
128: 
129: > [!TIP]
130: > - For a complete project show walkthrough, oral defense script, and architectural Q&A, refer to the **[Presentation Guide](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/PRESENTATION_GUIDE.md)**.
131: > - For automated one-click dependency installation, automated build scripts, and offline tools, check out [`Project.MM/setup/`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/setup) and [`Project.MM/setup/SETUP_GUIDE.md`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/setup/SETUP_GUIDE.md).
132: 
133: ---
134: 
135: ## Step-by-Step Simulation Execution
136: 
137: ### Step 1: Open the Project in VS Code
138: Open the directory `Project.MM/LocalConfig` directly in VS Code (`File` > `Open Folder...`). This ensures PlatformIO immediately detects `platformio.ini` and Wokwi automatically loads [`wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml).
139: 
140: > [!NOTE]
141: > **If VS Code was opened at the repo root (`Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab`)** instead of `Project.MM/LocalConfig`, make sure Wokwi uses [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml) by pressing `F1` $\rightarrow$ **`Wokwi: Select Config File`** (or reopen `Project.MM/LocalConfig` directly as the workspace folder). Otherwise, Wokwi may fail to load the `[net]` gateway setting or the compiled firmware binary.
142: 
143: ### Step 2: Compile the Firmware
144: - Click the **PlatformIO Build checkmark (✓)** on the bottom blue status bar, or press `Ctrl + Alt + B`.
145: - PlatformIO will download toolchains and libraries on first run, compiling to `.pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin`.

## Step-by-Step Simulation Execution

### Step 1: Open the Project in VS Code
Open the directory `Project.MM/LocalConfig` directly in VS Code (`File` > `Open Folder...`). This ensures PlatformIO immediately detects `platformio.ini` and Wokwi automatically loads [`wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml).

> [!NOTE]
> **If VS Code was opened at the repo root (`Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab`)** instead of `Project.MM/LocalConfig`, make sure Wokwi uses [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml) by pressing `F1` $\rightarrow$ **`Wokwi: Select Config File`** (or reopen `Project.MM/LocalConfig` directly as the workspace folder). Otherwise, Wokwi may fail to load the `[net]` gateway setting or the compiled firmware binary.

### Step 2: Compile the Firmware
- Click the **PlatformIO Build checkmark (✓)** on the bottom blue status bar, or press `Ctrl + Alt + B`.
- PlatformIO will download toolchains and libraries on first run, compiling to `.pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin`.

### Step 3: Configure Windows Firewall (One-Click)
To ensure client devices (such as smartphones and lab desktop PCs) can reach port 9080:
- Double-click [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) (or run from terminal).
- Accept the Windows UAC elevation prompt. The script configures inbound TCP port 9080 across all network profiles automatically.

### Step 4: Launch Network Gateway (wokwigw)
In a terminal window (PowerShell) inside `Project.MM/LocalConfig`:
```powershell
.\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
```
*(Leave this running in the background. It forwards host port 9080 into the simulated ESP32 port 80).*

### Step 5: Launch Wokwi Simulation
1. Open `diagram.json` in the VS Code editor.
2. Press `F1` (or `Ctrl + Shift + P`) to open the Command Palette.
3. Run: **`Wokwi: Start Simulator`** (or click the green Play button).
4. Watch the integrated Serial Monitor output:
   ```text
   --------------------------------------------------
     [PHASE 1 EXECUTION] Mounting MicroSD via VSPI   
   --------------------------------------------------
   [PHASE 1 SUCCESS] FAT32 Storage Mounted.
   [PHASE 1 CAPACITY] Total: 8 MB | Used: ...
   [PHASE 1 STORAGE] Seeded /www/index.html
   [PHASE 1 STORAGE] Seeded /lab_report.txt
   [PHASE 2 NET] Wi-Fi Connected!
   [PHASE 2 NET] Node IP Address: 10.13.37.2
   [PHASE 2 HTTP] Server active and listening on port 80.
   ```

## Simultaneous Multi-Interface Access (Ethernet LAN + Wi-Fi Hotspot)

### Why Multi-Interface Works (0.0.0.0:9080 Binding)
When you start the gateway using:
```powershell
.\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
```
The gateway binary does **not** bind strictly to `127.0.0.1`. Instead, it binds to socket `0.0.0.0:9080` (INADDR_ANY), meaning it actively listens on **every network interface enabled on your Windows host PC**.

This allows you to serve the simulated ESP32 NAS simultaneously across both wired and wireless networks!

```
                       +---------------------------------------+
                       |   Host Workstation (0.0.0.0:9080)    |
                       |       wokwigw.exe TCP Forwarder       |
                       +-------------------+-------------------+
                                           |
                    +----------------------+----------------------+
                    |                                             |
                    ▼                                             ▼
       [Wired Ethernet Interface]                    [Windows Mobile Hotspot]
        IP: e.g. 192.168.1.105                         Virtual IP: 192.168.137.1
                    |                                             |
                    ▼                                             ▼
          Lab Desktop PCs on LAN                       Smartphones & Tablets
    http://192.168.1.105:9080/                      http://192.168.137.1:9080/
```

### Method A: Wireless Access via Windows Mobile Hotspot
To allow smartphones, tablets, and external laptops to connect wirelessly without lab router credentials:
1. Open Windows **Settings > Network & internet > Mobile hotspot**.
2. Select **Share my internet connection from**: `Ethernet` (or `Wi-Fi`).
3. Set **Share over**: `Wi-Fi`.
4. Turn **Mobile hotspot** to **ON**.
5. Note your hotspot Network Name (SSID) and Password.
6. Connect external smartphones or tablets to this hotspot.
7. Windows automatically assigns the host PC an IP of **`192.168.137.1`** on the virtual hotspot adapter.
8. On the connected phone/tablet, open any mobile browser and navigate to:
   - **`http://192.168.137.1:9080/`** (NAS Dashboard)
   - **`http://192.168.137.1:9080/site`** (Static Webpage)

### Method B: Wired Access via Physical Ethernet LAN Switch
To allow lab PCs on the local campus network switch to access the node:
1. Ensure your host machine is connected to the lab Ethernet switch/wall port.
2. Open PowerShell and find your local Ethernet IPv4 address:
   ```powershell
   ipconfig
   ```
   *(Look for `IPv4 Address` under Ethernet adapter, e.g., `192.168.1.105` or `10.100.x.x`).*
3. From any other lab desktop PC connected to the same switch/subnet, open the browser and navigate to:
   - **`http://<YOUR_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/`** (e.g. `http://192.168.1.105:9080/`)
   - **`http://<YOUR_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/site`**

---

### Endpoint & Host IP Mapping Table

Use this reference table to access the appropriate endpoints during your live lab evaluation:

| Interface Type | Connected Client Device | Host IP Reference | NAS Explorer URL | Hosted Static Site URL |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Localhost (Loopback)** | Host PC (Where VS Code is running) | `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` | [http://localhost:9080/](http://localhost:9080/) | [http://localhost:9080/site](http://localhost:9080/site) |
| **Windows Mobile Hotspot** | Evaluator smartphones, tablets, laptops | `192.168.137.1` *(Default Windows Hotspot Gateway)* | `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` | `http://192.168.137.1:9080/site` |
| **Wired Ethernet LAN** | Lab workstation PCs on campus switch | `<YOUR_LAN_IP>` *(From `ipconfig`)* | `http://<YOUR_LAN_IP>:9080/` | `http://<YOUR_LAN_IP>:9080/site` |

---

## Local Network File Sharing (LocalSend Web Model)

### Workflow: Sharing Files Between Two Lab Computers
Just like the **"Share via Browser" (Web Share)** mode in **LocalSend**, `Project.MM` enables zero-installation local network file exchange between two lab computers or workstations via a standard web browser:

```text
 [Lab PC 1: Host Node]                                 [Lab PC 2: Peer Client]
 +----------------------------------+                  +----------------------------------+
 | Wokwi Simulator (ESP32 DevKit)   |                  | Standard Web Browser             |
 |   ↕ (WS: ws://localhost:9011)    |                  | (Chrome / Edge / Firefox)        |
 | wokwigw.exe (0.0.0.0:9080)       |                  |                                  |
 | Windows Firewall Port 9080 OPEN  |                  | Navigates to:                    |
 +-----------------+----------------+                  | http://<PC1_IP>:9080/            |
                   |                                   +-----------------+----------------+
                   |                                                     |
                   +=================== LAN SWITCH =====================+
                               (or Windows Mobile Hotspot)
```

1. **Host Setup (PC 1)**: Runs the Wokwi simulation with `wokwigw.exe` and opens `http://localhost:9080/` (or `http://<PC1_IP>:9080/`).
2. **Peer Connection (PC 2)**: Without installing any desktop apps, PC 2 opens its browser and navigates to `http://<PC1_IP>:9080/`.
3. **Bi-directional Sharing**:
   - PC 1 uploads a file (e.g., `labtest2A.asm`) $\rightarrow$ Stored in the MicroSD FAT32 filesystem $\rightarrow$ PC 2 refreshes and clicks **Download**.
   - PC 2 selects a file (e.g., `lab_report.txt`) in the upload box $\rightarrow$ Uploads directly to the ESP32 storage $\rightarrow$ PC 1 refreshes and downloads it.
4. **Real-Time Storage Telemetry**: Both computers see the dynamic storage capacity progress bar update in real-time as files are written and deleted.

---

### Architectural Comparison: Project.MM vs. LocalSend Web

While the front-end user experience mirrors LocalSend Web, the underlying embedded systems architecture fulfills the hardware requirements of `CSE0611324`:

| Dimension | LocalSend Web ("Share via Browser") | Project.MM Embedded NAS (`LocalConfig`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Compute Engine** | Heavy OS desktop application (Flutter / Rust / Dart on PC with 16 GB RAM) | **Classic ESP32 MCU** (Xtensa 32-bit Dual-Core LX6 @ 240 MHz, 520 KB SRAM) |
| **Storage Architecture** | Standard OS filesystem calls to PC NVMe/SSD drive | **Hardware VSPI Bus (SCK:18, MISO:19, MOSI:23, CS:5)** driving raw FAT32 SD block sectors |
| **Memory Budget** | Megabytes to gigabytes allocated in OS heap buffers | **Strict ~2 KB Streaming Window**: multipart upload chunks and download streams never overload SRAM |
| **Host Independence** | **Host-dependent**: If PC 1 closes the LocalSend window, sharing terminates immediately | **Independent Appliance**: The ESP32 is a standalone network node. Both PC 1 and PC 2 are equal clients connecting to external hardware |
| **Additional Services** | File transfer only | **Dual Service**: Simultaneous NAS file server + hosted static web node (`/site` streaming `/www/index.html` from SD card) |

---

### Lab Demonstration Checklist

1. **Firewall Rule**: On PC 1, execute [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator.
2. **Start Gateway**: In PowerShell, run:
   ```powershell
   .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
   ```
3. **Start Simulation**: Open [`diagram.json`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/diagram.json), press `F1`, and select **`Wokwi: Start Simulator`**.
4. **Find Host IP**: Run `ipconfig` on PC 1 to get its IPv4 address (e.g., `192.168.1.105` on LAN or `192.168.137.1` on Hotspot).
5. **Access from PC 2**: Open browser on PC 2 and navigate to `http://<PC1_IP>:9080/`.
6. **Exchange Files**: Upload from PC 1 $\rightarrow$ download from PC 2; upload from PC 2 $\rightarrow$ download from PC 1.

---

## Access Endpoints

Once `wokwigw` and the simulation are active, the web endpoints provide:
- **NAS File Manager Dashboard (`/`)**: Displays real-time FAT32 storage capacity meter, file list, file upload form, and file delete buttons.
- **Hosted Static Webpage (`/site`)**: Streams `/www/index.html` stored on the virtual MicroSD card.
- **Direct File Download (`/get?file=<name>`)**: Streams requested files in binary octet-stream mode directly to the client device.
- **Multipart Upload (`/upload`)**: Streams client files chunk-by-chunk into MicroSD FAT32 storage with ~2 KB RAM overhead.

---

## Troubleshooting & Tips

- **`connect tcp 10.13.37.2:80: no route to host` Error**:
  - **Cause**: The Wokwi simulator did not connect to `wokwigw`'s internal WebSocket server (`ws://localhost:9011`), meaning the virtual ESP32 is not registered in the gateway's network table.
  - **Fix**:
    1. Ensure `wokwi.toml` includes:
       ```toml
       [net]
       gateway = "ws://localhost:9011"
       ```
    2. **Start `wokwigw.exe` FIRST** in a separate terminal:
       ```powershell
       .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
       ```
    3. **Then Restart the Wokwi Simulation**: In VS Code, open `diagram.json`, press `F1`, and run `Wokwi: Restart Simulator` (or `Start Simulator`).
    4. In the `wokwigw` terminal, you should see confirmation of a connected client / DHCP lease.
    5. Wait until the Serial Monitor displays:
       ```text
       [WIFI] Connected!
       [NET] Node IP Address: 10.13.37.2
       ```
    6. Only now open `http://localhost:9080/` in your browser.

- **External Clients Cannot Connect (Connection Timed Out)**:
  - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator to verify Windows Firewall permits TCP port 9080 on Private and Public network profiles.
- **IP Mismatch**: The standard Wokwi gateway subnet is `10.13.37.2`. If your Serial Monitor displays a different node IP address, adjust the forwarding argument: `--forward 9080:<node-ip>:80`.
